title: SIU report reveals new shootout details
article: One investigation has ended and another isbeginning into the deadly meeting between Fred Preston and Constable Vu Pham onMarch 8.

Ontario's Special Investigation Unit has concluded itsinvestigation into the death of Fred Preston by stating it can find no groundsfor any criminal charges. The next day the Chief Coroner of Ontario announcedan inquest into the two men's death.

Preston, a long-time Sundridge area resident and the formerreeve of Joly Township, and Pham, an OPP constable, were both killed in ashootout on a country road in southern Ontario near the town of Wingham inHuron County. Pham lived in Sundridge for a brief time and several of hissiblings still live in Almaguin.

The SIU states in a press release that Pham and anotherofficer were responding to a dispatch to Preston's sister-in-law's home. Theywere told there was reason to believe Preston may be there with the intentionto do harm to his sister-in-law, "in retaliation for his wife leaving him."
However, when the officers arrived, in separate cars, therewas no one home and they left but stayed in the area.

It was at 10:12 a.m. that Pham spotted Preston's vehicle andradioed the other officer for assistance. He then signaled for Preston, drivinga white pickup truck, to pull over. Preston did and Pham parked his cruiserabout eight feet behind the truck. As he and Preston exited their vehicles theother officer, identified by the Canadian Press as Constable Del Mercy, pulledup to the scene with the intention of pulling in behind Pham's cruiser.However, as he was coming to a stop he saw Preston pull the rifle from thetruck and walk to the back of it before raising it and shooting Pham. He saw Phamunholster his sidearm and he managed to fire it, "once immediately before beingfelled but it is unlikely that this shot hit Mr. Preston," reads the SIUreport.

Mercy then backed his cruiser about 100 feet away fromPreston before stopping and getting out of his vehicle. Preston is said to havetaken two shots, with a Browning 30-06 at Mercy before he was able to unholsterhis own sidearm and return fire.

The shots being fired at him didn't slow Preston down, whoadvanced towards the officer eventually prompting him to back away from hisposition beside his cruiser. During this part of the stand off, Mercy lost hisfooting and Preston fired another shot at him before turning towards the ditchfor cover. From the roadway, Mercy fired five more shots at Preston anddisabled him. When other officers arrived at the scene they found Preston wasstill conscious despite being hit six times. Mercy was not struck.
Both Pham and Preston were airlifted from the scene to ahospital in London where they would both die - Pham that day and Preston threedays later.
Director of the SIU Ian Scott stated in his report thatMercy was justified under the Criminal Code to shoot Preston.

"Here, the subject officer had witnessed the gratuitouskilling of a fellow police officer and the same assailant shooting at him. AsMr. Preston walked toward the officer, he discharged another round in hisdirection... There was simply nowhere he could go to find protection frompotentially imminent death or grievous harm. Accordingly, in my view, he hadreasonable grounds to believe he had no choice but to continue shooting."
Even more details of the deadly confrontation could berevealed sometime next year when the coroner's inquest is conducted.
During that process a jury will listen to testimony aboutthe circumstances around the encounter and whether there are any measures thatmay prevent a similar tragedy.
The inquest will look into both Pham and Preston's deathseven though it is Preston's death that is making the inquest mandatory.

"The Office (of the Coroner) considers the circumstances inwhich Mr. Preston came to his death to be mandatory for an inquest. We considerhim to be in police custody when he died," said Cheryl Mahyr, issues managerfor the Office of the Chief Coroner and the Ontario Forensic Pathology Service.
She said the inquest is just beginning the planning stageand doubts that it would be conducted this year. Outside of that, Mahyr said itwould be difficult to predict when it may happen.
"There is no rule as to when (inquests) are held... Sometimesit can take over 12 months, sometimes five years," said Mahyr.

Before an inquest can be called by the chief coroner, it hasto be established that there are no outstanding charges relating to theincident to be studied. In the Preston/Pham case, the SIU completing itsinvestigation was the end of that process.

Mahyr describes the inquest process as being similar to atrial where counsel will represent the coroner and interested parties canpetition to be represented and have counsel cross-examine. She also says that astrong effort will be made to hold the inquest near where the incidentoccurred.
